title: Strategy into Execution
question: Why do sound strategies so often fail to change what an organization actually does, and how should a leader sequence change so that it takes hold?

overview.text: The first eleven weeks asked how to think, how people behave, how to weigh evidence, how organizations hold power, and how to choose strategies and justify them financially and legally. This week asks the question that decides whether any of that matters: how does a choice become a changed pattern of work? Most leaders discover that announcing a strategy is easy and changing what hundreds of people do on an ordinary Tuesday is hard.

The week moves through four lenses. Lesson 1 examines why execution fails—less through defiance than through weak coordination across units, resources that never move, and improvement time eaten by daily pressure. Lesson 2 audits the change-management canon: the famous “70 per cent of change fails” statistic, Kotter’s eight steps, the three-step model credited to Lewin, and the more diagnosable idea of readiness. Lesson 3 brings in operations—Little’s law, bottlenecks, variability and Toyota’s standard work—because every change is also a flow of work through scarce people. Lesson 4 crosses borders: what cultural frameworks can and cannot tell you, why institutions matter, and how to decide what must be identical across sites and what each site should own.

The Change Simulator asks you to sequence a four-hospital rollout under time, budget and trust constraints. The case follows a manufacturer implementing one system across plants in three countries. The assignment is a 90-day implementation roadmap for a change of your own choosing. Throughout, the standard is the same as in Week 4: popular frameworks are useful, but know which ones are evidence and which are heuristics.

objectives: Diagnose a stalled initiative using evidence about resource allocation, cross-unit coordination and improvement time rather than stated priorities.
Evaluate popular change models and statistics, distinguishing practitioner heuristics from tested findings.
Assess readiness for change as commitment and efficacy, and match interventions to each.
Apply Little’s law, bottleneck logic and leading and lagging indicators to design an operating rhythm for a change.
Design a multi-site rollout that separates core components from adaptable periphery and accounts for institutional differences.
Produce a 90-day implementation roadmap with phases, decision points, stakeholders, metrics and risks.

lessons.title: Why Execution Fails: The Gap Between Choosing and Doing
lessons.summary: Strategies stall less because people disobey than because coordination, reallocation and improvement time are starved by the daily operation.
objectives: Explain the strategy–execution gap as a problem of coordination, reallocation and attention rather than compliance.
Diagnose a stalled initiative using resource-allocation evidence instead of stated priorities.
Describe the capability trap and why it leads managers to blame people for system problems.
lessons.executive: Most strategies do not fail in the boardroom; they fade in the calendar. Large manager surveys suggest that alignment up and down the hierarchy is usually adequate, while coordination across units, reallocation of money and people, and shared understanding of priorities are weak. Meanwhile, daily pressure diverts time from improvement work, capability erodes, and leaders blame effort rather than the system. Before announcing a new initiative, audit where people, money and senior attention actually go, name what will stop, and protect time for building capability. Treat your stated priorities as hypotheses that your budget and calendar must confirm.

explore.text: Consider a hypothetical regional bank that announces a “digital-first” strategy. The annual report features the strategy, the chief executive repeats it at every town hall, and each division adds a digital objective to its scorecard. Three years later, branch staffing is nearly unchanged, the mobile-app team is still borrowing engineers from the core-systems group during every quarter-end, and the most experienced relationship managers have been told the strategy matters but are still paid on in-branch loan volume. Nobody refused the strategy. Nobody sabotaged it. It simply never received the people, money and attention that its words implied.

Before reading on, rank these explanations for the bank’s stall from most to least likely: (a) employees resisted the strategy; (b) the strategy was poorly communicated; (c) resources and incentives were never reallocated; (d) units that needed each other could not coordinate. Write down your ranking and one piece of evidence that would distinguish your top two.

Most executives instinctively choose resistance or communication. Those explanations are flattering to the strategy and convenient for the leader: if the problem is that people did not listen, the remedy is more messaging. This lesson argues that the more common culprits are less visible—coordination across units, reallocation of scarce resources, and the slow erosion of capability when everyone is too busy to improve. These are properties of the system, which means they are the executive’s responsibility rather than the frontline’s.

understand.text: Strategy is what you fund, staff and pay attention to

A useful working definition for this week: a strategy is a set of choices about where to compete and how, and its *realized* form is the pattern of resource allocation that actually occurs. A plan describes intended activities; a budget assigns money; a calendar assigns attention. When the three disagree, the calendar and the budget usually win. This is why an execution diagnosis should start by reading the allocation record—headcount moves, capital approvals, meeting agendas, promotion decisions—rather than the strategy document.

understand.title: Prerequisite: strategy, plan, budget and operating rhythm

blocks.text: Four terms are often blurred. *Strategy* is the small number of choices that define how an organization intends to win or create value. A *plan* sequences the activities that implement those choices. A *budget* commits money and headcount for a period. An *operating rhythm* is the recurring set of meetings, reviews and reports through which the organization notices problems and decides. Execution happens when all four point the same way; the gap opens when the strategy changes but the budget, the plan and the rhythm stay the same.
A quick test: name the three largest reallocations of people or money made in the past year. If none of them follows from the stated strategy, the strategy is aspirational, not operational.

understand.text: Five beliefs about execution, and what survey evidence suggests

Donald Sull, Rebecca Homkes and Charles Sull reported on a multi-year survey program of managers across several hundred companies. Their central argument is that common executive beliefs about execution are wrong or incomplete. Alignment within the reporting line was usually reasonable; the weak link was coordination *across* functions and units. They report that only about one in ten managers said they could always rely on colleagues in other functions and units, and that only about 55 percent of the middle managers surveyed could name even one of their company’s top five priorities despite frequent communication. Treat these figures as descriptive results from one survey population, not as universal base rates.

Rewards often favor hitting own numbers over helping other units
Make cross-unit help visible and rewarded
Execution should be driven from the top
Distributed middle managers make most execution decisions
Give middle managers decision rules, not just targets

understand.text: The capability trap

Nelson Repenning and John Sterman studied organizations that adopted well-proven improvement methods yet failed to sustain them. Their explanation is a self-reinforcing loop. When performance falls short of target, people can close the gap in two ways: work harder (more hours, more firefighting, cutting corners) or work smarter (invest time in improving the process). Working harder pays off immediately; working smarter pays off later and initially costs output. Under pressure, people choose working harder, the time available for improvement shrinks, the underlying capability of the process decays, and performance falls further—which increases the pressure.

understand.caption: The capability trap as a causal chain (after Repenning and Sterman, 2001)

steps.label: Performance gap
steps.text: Results fall short of the target set by leadership.

steps.label: Work harder
steps.text: Time shifts from improvement to firefighting; quick gains appear.

steps.label: Capability erodes
steps.text: Maintenance, training and process fixes are deferred.

steps.label: Gap widens
steps.text: Defects and rework rise, so performance slips again.

steps.label: Blame people
steps.text: Leaders attribute shortfalls to effort and tighten control, restarting the loop.

understand.text: The last link is the most important for executives. Repenning and Sterman argue that managers tend to attribute performance problems to the people doing the work rather than to the system they work within. That attribution makes the trap self-sealing: when leaders believe the problem is effort, they increase monitoring and pressure, which further crowds out improvement and confirms their belief.
Attention is the scarcest resource

Money and headcount are visible in budgets; senior attention is not, yet it is often the binding constraint. An initiative competes for the agenda of the weekly leadership meeting, for the first hour of a manager’s day, and for the questions the chief executive asks. A practical rule of thumb: an initiative that does not appear on a recurring agenda, with a named owner and a metric reviewed at a fixed interval, has been allocated no attention, whatever the strategy document says. This is an APERTURE heuristic, not a research finding, but it is easy to test in your own organization.

challenge.text: The execution-failure literature has its own weaknesses, and an evidence-minded leader should hold them in view.

items: **The line between strategy and execution is blurry.** A strategy that cannot be executed with the organization’s real capabilities is arguably a bad strategy, not a good strategy badly executed. Calling every disappointment an “execution problem” protects the strategists.

**Survey evidence describes perceptions.** Managers who report poor coordination may be describing real problems, or explaining their own disappointing results. Without comparison groups or outcome data, survey patterns show what managers believe, not what causes success.

**Case-based mechanisms can be over-applied.** The capability trap is a compelling story built from field studies and simulation models. It explains many stalls, but not all: sometimes performance falls because people genuinely lack skill or motivation, and sometimes a process truly cannot be improved further.

**Agility can become an excuse.** Reallocating resources whenever conditions change can turn into strategy drift. The useful question is not whether to adapt but which signals justify a reallocation, decided in advance.

challenge.title: Methodological note: what a manager survey can and cannot tell you

blocks.text: Large practitioner surveys are valuable for describing the landscape: how often managers report a problem, and in which kinds of firms. They are weak for causal claims, for three reasons. First, *common-method bias*: when the same respondent rates both the cause (for example, coordination) and the outcome (execution quality), shared mood or self-presentation inflates the correlation. Second, *selection*: firms that agree to participate in a consultancy-linked survey may differ from those that do not. Third, *reverse causation*: an initiative that is already failing may make people perceive coordination as poor.

Stronger designs would compare units that adopted a coordination practice with similar units that did not, ideally with objective outcome measures and data collected before and after. Such studies are rare in strategy execution, which is a reason to treat practitioner findings as well-informed hypotheses to test in your own setting.

apply.text: A hypothetical health system adopts the strategy of reducing avoidable readmissions. The chief medical officer asks you to explain why, a year later, the readmission rate has not moved. Rather than surveying staff about their commitment, you run a four-part execution audit.

apply.caption: An execution audit for a stalled initiative (APERTURE teaching device)
headers: What a stall typically looks like
rows: Headcount, budget and schedule changes since launch
New goal, same staffing; care coordinators added on paper but borrowed for ward coverage
Process map from discharge to first follow-up visit
Pharmacy, outpatient clinics and social work each optimize their own queue
Agendas of the last eight leadership meetings

Hours per week staff spend on redesign versus firefighting
Improvement meetings cancelled during every census surge

apply.text: The audit converts a vague complaint—“people aren’t executing”—into specific, fixable conditions. In this example, the remedy is not another campaign but three decisions: assign the care coordinators exclusively to the initiative, create a weekly cross-unit huddle with authority to fix hand-off problems, and protect a fixed block of improvement time even during surges, accepting a short-term cost.

apply.title: Executive twist: the board wants a date

blocks.text: The board asks for a firm date by which readmissions will fall by a stated amount. You know that protecting improvement time will first *lower* throughput and may make the next two quarters look worse. Committing to an aggressive date invites the capability trap; refusing to commit looks evasive. A defensible middle course is to commit to leading indicators on a short horizon (coordinator coverage, hand-off completion) and to the outcome on a longer horizon, explaining the expected dip in advance so that it reads as the plan working rather than failing.

apply.text: **Professional application.** A player development department announces that every player will have an individualized development plan. Six months later, plans exist as documents, but coach-to-player ratios, travel schedules and the weekly staff meeting are unchanged, and the strength, medical, analytics and coaching groups still review players in separate meetings. Applying the audit: what was reallocated to make individual planning possible; where do the departments hand players off to each other; how often does the plan appear on a recurring agenda with a decision attached; and when the season gets busy, is plan-review time the first thing cancelled? The likely finding is a coordination and attention gap, not coach resistance.

retain.text: Execution fails most often in the spaces between units and in the slow erosion of improvement time, not through open defiance. Read the budget, the calendar and the hand-offs before you read the strategy document. When performance falls short, check whether pressure is consuming the very time needed to build capability, and be suspicious of any diagnosis that blames people first.
Without looking back: name three of the five execution beliefs challenged by Sull and colleagues, and the alternative they propose for each.
Draw the capability trap from memory as a loop of five or six links. Which link would you break first in an organization you know, and what would it cost in the short run?
Pick one priority your organization has announced in the last year. What three pieces of allocation evidence would show whether it is real?

takeaways: A strategy’s realized form is its pattern of resource allocation; audit budgets, calendars and hand-offs, not slogans.
Survey evidence suggests vertical alignment is usually adequate; cross-unit coordination and reallocation are the weak links.
The capability trap: pressure to produce crowds out improvement, capability erodes, and leaders wrongly blame effort.
Practitioner execution findings are well-informed hypotheses, not causal proof—test them locally.

check.prompt: An initiative has a named sponsor, a slide in every town hall and a goal on every scorecard, but no headcount has moved and it never appears on the weekly operating agenda. Which conclusion is best supported?

The initiative has received communication but not resources or attention, so its realized priority is low.
Employees are resisting the initiative and need clearer consequences.
The initiative needs a stronger slogan to break through.

check.explanation: Realized strategy shows in allocation: people, money and recurring attention. Communication without reallocation produces awareness but not execution, so the evidence points to a low realized priority rather than resistance.

optionFeedback.c: Nothing in the evidence indicates resistance; blaming people first is the attribution error Repenning and Sterman warn about.
optionFeedback.d: More messaging repeats the “communication equals understanding” belief; the gap is allocation.

check.prompt: Which observations are consistent with an organization caught in the capability trap? Select all that apply.

options.text: Improvement meetings are routinely cancelled when workload spikes.
Overtime has risen while rework and defects have also risen.
Leaders respond to missed targets by adding monitoring of individual staff.
The team deliberately accepted a one-quarter output dip to redesign a process.
Short-term output gains followed by a slow decline in underlying performance.

check.explanation: The trap combines crowding out of improvement time (a), working harder while capability decays (b, e), and attributing shortfalls to people, which increases control (c). Option d is the escape route: protecting improvement time at a short-term cost.

lessons.title: Change Models and the Evidence Behind Them
lessons.summary: The most popular change models are useful practitioner checklists with thin evidence, while readiness—commitment plus efficacy—gives you something you can actually diagnose.
objectives: Evaluate the evidence behind the claim that 70 per cent of change initiatives fail.
Distinguish Kotter’s eight steps and the Lewin three-step model as practitioner heuristics from tested theory.
Diagnose readiness for change as two separate states—commitment and efficacy—and match interventions to each.
Treat resistance as information about the change, not only as an obstacle.
lessons.executive: You will hear that 70 per cent of change efforts fail; the claim has no valid empirical base and mostly serves to manufacture urgency. The best-known change models—Kotter’s eight steps and the “unfreeze–change–refreeze” sequence attributed to Lewin—are practitioner heuristics. Use them as checklists, not as science; the three-step model was not even developed by Lewin in the form usually taught. A more diagnosable idea is readiness: do people want this change (commitment), and do they believe they can do it (efficacy)? Low commitment and low efficacy need different remedies. Read resistance as data about the design before treating it as a problem of attitude.

explore.text: Open almost any change-management presentation and you will find, near the beginning, the claim that about 70 per cent of organizational change initiatives fail. The number does useful rhetorical work: it makes change sound difficult, justifies investment in specialists and creates urgency. It is also, as far as anyone has been able to show, unsupported.

Before reading on: if 70 per cent of change initiatives really failed, what would someone have had to measure to know it? Write down the denominator (failure out of *what*?), the definition of failure, and when it would be measured.

Mark Hughes traced the 70 per cent figure through five frequently cited published sources and concluded that, although the narrative of 70 per cent failure is widespread, there is no valid and reliable empirical evidence for it. Some of the sources concerned narrower programs such as business-process reengineering; others presented the figure without describing how it was obtained.

This does not mean change usually succeeds. It means nobody knows the base rate, partly because “change initiative” and “failure” are almost never defined consistently. An executive who cites the number to a board is borrowing authority from a statistic that does not exist. The more interesting question is which features of a change predict its fate in *your* setting—and that is where the models come in.

understand.title: Prerequisite: what would it mean for a change to fail?

blocks.text: Failure can mean at least four different things: the change was never implemented as designed (an *implementation* failure); it was implemented but did not produce the intended results (an *effectiveness* failure); it produced results that later faded (a *sustainability* failure); or it achieved its goals at a cost—in trust, turnover or side effects—that outweighed them. A change can succeed on one definition and fail on another. When someone quotes a failure rate, ask which definition they mean and who judged it.

understand.text: Two staged models and their status

The most famous change model is the three-step sequence of unfreezing, changing and refreezing, usually credited to the social psychologist Kurt Lewin. Stephen Cummings, Todd Bridgman and Kenneth Brown compared Lewin’s writings with later presentations and argue that he never developed such a model: its familiar form took shape after his death in 1947, while his actual work on group dynamics and action research was more iterative. Kotter’s eight steps—published in 1995 as eight errors observed in transformation efforts—are similarly an experience-based synthesis rather than a tested theory. Both remain popular because they are memorable and draw attention to real problems.

Manufactured crises that erode trust when exposed
Secure people with authority and credibility
A coalition of senior allies with no frontline credibility
A vision that substitutes for a diagnosis
Empowerment without resources or decision rights
6. Plan for and create short-term wins
Easy wins that avoid the root cause
Keep going after the first wins

Locking in a design before it has been tested
understand.note: Practitioner heuristic, not a validated sequence.

understand.text: Readiness: commitment and efficacy

A more precise, measurable idea comes from implementation science. Bryan Weiner defines organizational readiness for change as a shared psychological state with two parts. *Change commitment* is members’ shared resolve to implement the change; it is strongest when people value the change, weaker when they comply because they feel obliged or have no choice. *Change efficacy* is their shared belief that they can carry it out, which depends on how they appraise the task, the resources available and the circumstances. Weiner also argues that many different strategies can raise readiness—there is no single best way.

understand.caption: A readiness diagnosis: commitment by efficacy (after Weiner, 2009)
cells: **Not ready.** Clarify the problem and test the design with the people affected before scaling anything.
**Capable skeptics.** Show evidence, involve them in design, address what they would lose.
**Willing but unsure.** Invest in training, tools, time and early practice; reduce task demands.
**Ready.** Move quickly, keep feedback loops open, guard against overconfidence.
understand.note: Teaching device; quadrant labels are APERTURE’s.

understand.text: The matrix matters because the remedies differ. More inspiring communication does little for a group that wants the change but believes it lacks the time or skills; training and protected practice do little for a group that does not see why the change is worth making. Many rollouts fail by applying the commitment remedy to an efficacy problem.
Resistance as information

People facing an ambiguous change construct a plausible account of what it means for them—whether they will be judged by a new metric, whether their expertise will still count, whether the change is a prelude to cuts. Resistance often reflects that account. Sometimes it is self-interest or habit. Often it contains information the designers lacked: a workflow the new system cannot handle, a hidden cost, a promise broken last time. A useful discipline is to classify each objection before responding: is it about the *content* of the change (the design is wrong), the *process* (people were not consulted or informed), or the *consequences* for the person (status, workload, job security)? Each needs a different answer, and only the first should change the design.

challenge.text: Is the staged-model tradition simply wrong? Not quite. Kotter’s list captures problems—weak coalitions, premature victory declarations—that many leaders recognize, and the eight steps remain a reasonable agenda for a planning conversation. The criticism is about status and pedigree: the models are presented as if they were established findings, when Kotter’s steps rest on the author’s observations and the three-step model attributed to Lewin is largely a later reconstruction. Hughes’s audit of the 70 per cent figure shows how a field can build on a number nobody measured.

items: **Linearity.** Staged models imply a sequence; real change loops back as designs are tested and revised.
**Top-down bias.** Both models are written from the change leader’s perspective; recipients appear mainly as sources of resistance.
**Survivorship.** Lessons drawn from memorable successes and failures ignore the many quiet changes that simply worked or quietly faded.
**Readiness is not destiny.** High readiness may produce effort without results if the change itself is a poor idea; readiness measures willingness and confidence, not wisdom.

challenge.title: Methodological note: why the base rate of change failure is nearly unmeasurable

blocks.text: To estimate a failure rate you need a defined population of change initiatives, a consistent definition of failure, and outcome data collected for all of them—not only for those that people remember. In practice, initiatives are not registered in advance, their goals shift during implementation, and success is judged retrospectively by the people who led them (who tend to recall success) or by consultants hired after trouble (who see failure). Each of these introduces bias in a different direction, and their net effect is unknown.

A better question is conditional: among initiatives *like this one*, in settings *like ours*, what predicted implementation and effect? Implementation science approaches this with prospective studies that define outcomes in advance and measure them at every site, which is slower and less quotable but far more useful.

apply.text: A hypothetical mid-sized law firm plans to introduce document-automation software that drafts first versions of routine agreements. Partners are enthusiastic about margins; associates fear lost training and billable hours; paralegals expect their roles to change most. A readiness diagnosis would ask each group two questions—do you want this, and do you believe your group can make it work?—and look at the pattern. Suppose associates score high on efficacy and low on commitment (they can use it but think it undermines their development), while paralegals score high on commitment and low on efficacy (they want it but lack training time). The two groups need different interventions: a redesigned training path for associates, protected learning time and early practice for paralegals.

“Nobody asked the people who draft these every day.”
Involve drafters in configuration; publish decisions
Redesign training so automation does not remove learning

blocks.text: Your chief executive wants to open the rollout by announcing that “70 per cent of transformations fail, so we must move fast.” You know the figure is unsupported. Correcting the CEO in public is costly; repeating the number risks credibility with skeptical professionals who may check it. A defensible approach is to offer a stronger opening grounded in your own evidence—the specific cost of the status quo in your organization—and to explain privately why the borrowed statistic is a liability. Urgency built on local facts survives scrutiny; urgency built on folklore does not.

apply.text: **Professional application.** Suppose a player development department wants coaches to adopt a new movement-assessment protocol. A readiness diagnosis might find veteran coaches high in efficacy but low in commitment (“I can run it; I don’t see what it adds to what my eyes tell me”) and newer coaches high in commitment but low in efficacy (“I want to use it; I don’t know how to turn the output into a drill”). The first group needs evidence and a role in deciding how the output informs coaching; the second needs worked examples and supervised practice. Opening with urgency about a league-wide “analytics gap” would address neither.

retain.text: The famous 70 per cent figure lacks a valid evidential base, and the best-known change models are practitioner heuristics whose pedigree is weaker than their popularity. Readiness—shared commitment and shared efficacy—is more diagnosable and points to different remedies for different groups. Resistance is often information about the design, the process or the consequences, and each deserves a different response.

Sketch the commitment–efficacy matrix and give one intervention for each quadrant.
Recall an objection to a change you led or experienced. Was it about content, process or consequences—and how did the response match?

takeaways: The claim that 70 per cent of change efforts fail has no valid and reliable empirical base; ask for definitions and denominators.
Kotter’s eight steps and the three-step model credited to Lewin are practitioner heuristics; use them as checklists, not as science.
Readiness has two parts—commitment and efficacy—with different remedies.
Classify resistance as content, process or consequence before responding; only content objections should change the design.

lessons.title: Operations: Flow, Bottlenecks, Variability and Standard Work
lessons.summary: A small set of operations ideas—Little’s law, bottlenecks, the cost of high utilization, and standard work as experiment—explains why most implementations clog and how to run them.
objectives: Use Little’s law to relate work-in-process, throughput and lead time in any workflow.
Explain why improving a non-bottleneck rarely improves output, and why queues explode as utilization approaches 100 per cent.
Describe standard work as a testable hypothesis, following Spear and Bowen’s account of the Toyota Production System.
Design an operating rhythm that pairs leading and lagging indicators.
lessons.executive: Every organization is a set of flows: patients, cases, contracts, code changes, player evaluations. Three rules govern them. Little’s law: average work-in-process equals throughput multiplied by average time in the system, so starting more work without finishing faster simply lengthens lead times. The bottleneck sets the pace: improvements elsewhere add little. And variability punishes high utilization: as a resource approaches full load, waiting time rises steeply. Toyota’s lesson is less about tools than about specifying work precisely so each deviation is visible and becomes an experiment. Run change through an operating rhythm with leading indicators you can act on weekly and lagging indicators that confirm results.

explore.text: A hypothetical software team of eight engineers has 40 work items “in progress.” The team completes about 10 items a week. Leadership, frustrated that features take too long, approves two more projects and asks everyone to “parallelize.” Two months later, the team is busier than ever and delivery times are longer.
Before reading on: estimate how long, on average, an item now spends in progress. What would happen to that time if the team started fewer items but finished at the same rate?

The answer is about four weeks—40 items divided by 10 per week—and it follows from an identity, not an opinion. Starting more work without increasing the completion rate adds to the queue and lengthens lead times. Many implementation programs fail in exactly this way: an organization launches six initiatives at once, each competing for the same scarce specialists, and is surprised when none finishes. The tools in this lesson come from operations management, but they apply to any flow of work, including the flow of change itself.

blocks.text: *Throughput* (λ) is the rate at which work is completed, such as cases per week. *Work-in-process* (L) is the number of items started but not finished. *Lead time* or *cycle time* (W) is how long an item spends from start to finish. *Utilization* is the share of available time a resource is busy. A *bottleneck* is the step with the least capacity relative to demand. A *queue* is work waiting for a resource. These definitions are simple, but most operational arguments go wrong because people use them loosely—for example, treating “busy” as if it meant “productive.”

understand.text: Little’s law

John Little proved in 1961 that, for a stable system observed over the long run, the average number of items in the system equals the average arrival (or completion) rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system: L = λW. The result requires no assumptions about the distribution of arrivals or service times, which is why it applies so widely. In his fiftieth-anniversary review, Little emphasizes its practical use in operations and computing and proves versions for finite observation periods, which is how managers actually observe systems.

understand.caption: Little’s law in four settings (hypothetical numbers)
understand.note: Hypothetical figures for illustration; the relationship is exact for long-run averages in a stable system.

understand.text: Bottlenecks set the pace

In a sequence of dependent steps, output can be no faster than the slowest step relative to its demand. Adding capacity anywhere else increases idle time or inventory, not output. This logic, popularized in the practitioner tradition often called the theory of constraints, yields a disciplined sequence: identify the constraint; get the most out of it (never let it sit idle or work on defective inputs); subordinate the other steps to its pace; only then add capacity; and look again, because the bottleneck will move. In change programs the bottleneck is frequently a person—the one data engineer, the one trainer who speaks both languages, the executive whose sign-off every decision needs.
Variability and the cost of full utilization

Leaders often aim to keep expensive people fully busy. In any system with variability—uneven arrivals, uneven task lengths—that goal is costly. Queueing theory shows that waiting time rises non-linearly as utilization approaches 100 per cent. The figure below uses the simplest textbook single-server queue to show the pattern; real systems differ in magnitude but share the shape.

understand.caption: Average wait before service, in multiples of the average task time, at different utilization levels (single-server textbook queue)
understand.note: Synthetic illustration computed from the standard single-server (M/M/1) queue, where average wait ÷ task time = u ÷ (1 − u). Real systems differ in magnitude.

understand.text: The managerial implication is uncomfortable: a resource with no slack cannot absorb surprises, and implementation is mostly surprises. Protecting some spare capacity at the bottleneck is not waste; it is what keeps lead times stable.
Standard work as a hypothesis

Steven Spear and Kent Bowen studied Toyota and its suppliers over several years and concluded that the system’s performance rests not on its visible tools but on tacit rules. In their account, all work is highly specified as to content, sequence, timing and outcome; every connection between a customer and a supplier inside the plant is direct and gives an unambiguous yes-or-no signal; the pathway for every product and service is simple and direct; and every improvement is made using the scientific method, under the guidance of a teacher, at the lowest possible level of the organization. Their central paradox is that rigid specification is what makes flexibility possible: because the expected result is explicit, any deviation is immediately visible and can be investigated as a failed prediction.

understand.caption: Standard work as an experiment loop (after Spear and Bowen, 1999)

steps.label: Specify
steps.text: Write down how the work should be done and what result it should produce.

steps.label: Predict
steps.text: The specification is a hypothesis: done this way, it will give this result.

steps.label: Observe
steps.text: Deviation is visible immediately because the expectation is explicit.

steps.label: Investigate
steps.text: The people doing the work, with a coach, find the cause where it occurred.

steps.label: Revise
steps.text: Update the standard; the new version is the next hypothesis.

understand.text: Operating rhythm and leading versus lagging indicators

An operating rhythm is the recurring cadence of short reviews—daily huddles, weekly operating reviews, monthly or quarterly strategy reviews—through which an organization notices deviations and decides. Each level needs indicators at the right speed. *Lagging indicators* measure outcomes you ultimately care about (readmissions, client retention, major-league performance of developed players) but arrive late and mix many causes. *Leading indicators* measure behaviors or conditions believed to drive those outcomes (follow-up calls completed within 48 hours, open defects older than a week, share of development sessions with a written objective) and can be acted on quickly. A leading indicator is only as good as its causal link to the outcome, which should itself be tested.

understand.caption: Pairing leading and lagging indicators in an operating rhythm (hypothetical examples)
rows: Share of patients with a discharge plan by day 2
Work-in-process per engineer; age of open defects
Lower WIP and faster fixes reduce incidents
Contracts waiting longer than ten days
Shorter queues improve service and cost
Share of sessions with a written, measurable objective
Skill change on validated measures over a season
Planned sessions produce more skill gain
understand.note: Hypothetical examples; the causal links are assumptions to be checked, not findings.

items: **Little’s law describes averages, not causes.** It tells you that lead time will fall if work-in-process falls at constant throughput; it does not tell you why throughput is low, and it holds only when the system is reasonably stable over the period measured.
**The bottleneck is not always visible.** In knowledge work, the constraint can be a decision-maker’s attention or a hand-off rule rather than a machine, and it may shift weekly.

**Copying tools is not copying the system.** Spear and Bowen argue that organizations which imitate visible Toyota practices without the underlying rules rarely reproduce the results. Many “lean” programs became sets of boards and slogans.

**Standardization can freeze bad practice or suppress judgment.** In professional work with high variation—complex surgery, litigation, coaching—over-specification can remove the discretion that experts need. Spear and Bowen’s answer is that standards should be specified by those doing the work and revised constantly, not imposed and frozen.
**Leading indicators invite gaming.** Once a leading indicator becomes a target, people may improve the number without the behavior it was meant to capture—the Goodhart problem from Week 8.

challenge.text: The capability trap from Lesson 1 also has an operations form. When a unit runs near full utilization, any improvement work pushes it into overload, so improvement is deferred, defects rise, and utilization climbs further. Repenning and Sterman’s cases suggest that sustaining improvement requires deliberately creating slack for it and tolerating a temporary drop in measured output.

challenge.title: Methodological note: when Little’s law holds—and when it misleads

blocks.text: Little’s law is an identity for long-run averages in a system where items that enter eventually leave and the system is not growing or shrinking without limit. Over a short window, or in a system that is filling up (a backlog growing every week), the simple ratio can mislead because items still in the system have not yet recorded their full time. Little’s finite-period versions address this by accounting for items present at the start and end of the window.

Two practical checks follow. First, measure L, λ and W over the same window and with the same definition of “in the system.” Second, if the backlog is trending up or down, report the trend alongside the ratio; a stable-looking average lead time can hide a queue that is quietly exploding.

apply.text: A hypothetical public benefits office has 2,400 claims open and decides about 400 a week, so the average claim waits about six weeks. A legislator demands three-week turnaround. Leadership’s first instinct is overtime. An operations diagnosis asks: Where is the bottleneck? Suppose it is the medical-evidence review, staffed by four specialists at near-full utilization, while intake and eligibility steps have spare capacity. Overtime across the whole office adds work upstream of the bottleneck and lengthens its queue. Better moves are to stop sending incomplete files to the specialists (quality at the constraint), shift routine evidence checks to trained generalists (offload the constraint), and limit the number of claims released into review at once.

Halving lead time at constant throughput requires halving work-in-process: from 2,400 to about 1,200 open claims. That target is concrete, measurable weekly, and directly tied to the outcome the legislator cares about.

**Professional application.** In a player development system, many flows behave like queues: biomechanics assessments waiting for analysis, video waiting for coach review, players waiting for an individualized plan after arrival, rehabilitation cases waiting for a return-to-play decision. If 18 players await full review and staff complete six a week, the average wait is three weeks—long enough for a player’s first month at a new level to pass without a plan. The bottleneck is often one person—the only analyst who can process a data type, or the only bilingual coordinator. Protecting that person’s time from meetings and ad hoc requests, and limiting how many new reviews are opened at once, may do more than hiring elsewhere. A weekly huddle that tracks the age of the oldest open review (leading) alongside seasonal skill change (lagging) turns this into an operating rhythm.

retain.text: Work-in-process equals throughput multiplied by lead time, so starting more without finishing faster only lengthens queues. The bottleneck sets the pace, and variability makes fully utilized resources slow. Toyota’s deeper lesson is that specifying work precisely turns every deviation into an experiment. An operating rhythm pairs leading indicators you can act on weekly with lagging indicators that confirm results—while testing whether the leading indicators really lead.
A team has 45 items in progress and completes 9 per week. What is the average lead time, and what must happen to work-in-process to cut it to three weeks at the same throughput?

takeaways: Little’s law (L = λW): at constant throughput, lead time falls only if work-in-process falls.
Improving a non-bottleneck rarely improves output; protect and offload the constraint first.
Waiting time rises steeply as utilization nears 100 per cent; slack at the bottleneck is not waste.
In Spear and Bowen’s account, standard work is a hypothesis that makes deviations visible and learning possible.
Pair leading indicators (weekly, actionable) with lagging indicators (outcomes), and test the link between them.

lessons.title: Implementation Across Cultures and Institutions
lessons.summary: Moving a practice across sites and countries succeeds when you hold the core constant, adapt the periphery, and diagnose institutions and context rather than relying on national stereotypes.
objectives: Use cultural-dimension frameworks with calibrated confidence, citing what meta-analytic evidence and critics say about them.
Explain institutional distance and the difference between implementing a practice and internalizing it.
Apply the CFIR domains to diagnose a multi-site rollout.
Separate an intervention’s core components from its adaptable periphery.
lessons.executive: When a practice that works at headquarters stalls abroad, leaders reach for national culture to explain it. Evidence suggests cultural values predict work outcomes only modestly, and national averages say little about a particular site or person. Institutions—laws, professional norms and taken-for-granted ways of working—often matter more, and they determine whether a practice is merely implemented or genuinely internalized. Use implementation frameworks such as CFIR to diagnose the intervention, the outer and inner settings, the individuals and the process. Decide in advance which components are core and must be faithful, and which are periphery that each site should adapt. Fidelity to purpose beats uniformity of form.

explore.text: A hypothetical global retailer introduces an “open-door escalation” policy: any employee who sees a safety or ethics problem should raise it directly with the regional director, bypassing the store manager. At its home-country stores, escalations rise and several serious problems are caught early. At stores in two other countries, escalations stay near zero for a year. The regional team concludes that employees there are “too deferential to hierarchy” and proposes mandatory training on speaking up.
Before reading on: list three explanations for the near-zero escalations other than national culture. What evidence would distinguish them from the deference explanation?

Possible alternatives include: local labor law or works agreements that make bypassing a manager risky; a recent history in which an employee who complained was dismissed; a translated policy that reads as an invitation to inform on colleagues; store managers who quietly discourage escalation; or simply that the regional director does not speak the local language. Each of these predicts the same silence and calls for a different remedy. National-culture explanations are tempting because they are available, flattering to headquarters and impossible to disprove in a single meeting.

blocks.text: *Culture*, in management research, usually means shared values, beliefs and norms of a group. *Institutions* are the rules of the game—formal laws and regulations, professional and occupational norms, and the taken-for-granted assumptions about how things are done. The two interact, but they are not the same: two neighboring sites can share a national culture and differ sharply in institutions (one unionized, one not; one regulated by a different licensing body), and one site can sit under a corporate rulebook that overrides local habit in some matters and not in others. Implementation problems are often institutional problems that get described as cultural ones.

understand.text: Cultural dimensions: useful priors, weak predictors

Geert Hofstede’s framework describes national cultures on a small number of dimensions—originally power distance, individualism versus collectivism, uncertainty avoidance, and masculinity versus femininity, with dimensions added later. Later frameworks, such as the GLOBE project, distinguish what people report their society *does* from what they believe it *should* do. These frameworks are widely taught because they offer a quick language for difference.

How well do they predict? Vas Taras, Bradley Kirkman and Piers Steel meta-analyzed 598 studies covering more than 200,000 individuals. Hofstede’s four original dimensions were related to organizational outcomes, but modestly (an overall absolute weighted correlation of about .18 at the individual level). Cultural values predicted emotions and attitudes better than behaviors, and job performance least well; they predicted performance, absenteeism and turnover less well than personality and demographics did, but organizational commitment and citizenship behavior better. Effects were larger in culturally “tighter” countries with stronger norms.

understand.caption: What the meta-analytic evidence supports—and does not—when using cultural dimensions in implementation (APERTURE synthesis of Taras et al., 2010, and McSweeney, 2002)
rows: Anticipating that attitudes toward hierarchy or uncertainty may differ across sites
Values relate to attitudes and emotions more than to behavior
Predicting how a specific employee or manager will react
Group averages say little about individuals; within-country variation is large
Explaining a single site’s poor adoption
Many institutional and local explanations predict the same pattern
Designing the core of a global practice around country scores
Effects are modest and other factors predict performance better

understand.text: Institutional distance: implemented versus internalized

Tatiana Kostova defines the success of transferring an organizational practice across countries as its *institutionalization* at the receiving unit: the practice is not only carried out as prescribed but comes to be seen by employees as valuable and legitimate. She proposes that transfer is harder the greater the *institutional distance* between home and host environments—differences in regulations, in shared cognitive frameworks, and in social norms—and that organizational culture and the relationships between units, such as trust and identification with the parent, also shape whether a practice takes hold.

understand.caption: Implementation versus internalization (after Kostova, 1999)
x: practice not carried out as prescribed
cells: **Rejected.** Neither done nor believed. Re-examine fit and the case for the change.
**Ceremonial.** Done on paper, privately dismissed. Audits look fine; results do not move.
**Latent support.** Believed in but blocked by rules, resources or systems. Remove the obstacles.
**Institutionalized.** Done and valued; survives leadership changes.
understand.note: Teaching device; quadrant labels are APERTURE’s.

understand.text: The ceremonial quadrant is the executive’s blind spot. Compliance metrics—training completed, forms filed, meetings held—show success while the practice is hollow. The only reliable test is behavior when no one is checking, and whether staff can explain why the practice matters in their own words.
A structured diagnosis: CFIR

Implementation science offers a disciplined checklist for multi-site work. Laura Damschroder and colleagues consolidated constructs from many published implementation theories into the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), organized in five domains: the characteristics of the intervention (including its adaptability), the *outer setting* (external pressures, policies, the needs of those served), the *inner setting* (structure, culture, readiness and resources of the implementing organization), the characteristics of the individuals involved, and the process of implementation (planning, engaging, executing, reflecting and evaluating). They distinguish an intervention’s *core components* from its *adaptable periphery*—the elements that can be tailored without undermining the intervention.

understand.caption: Applying the five CFIR domains to a three-site rollout (hypothetical questions)
rows: Which components produce the benefit, and which are packaging we could change?
Which laws, regulators, unions, professional bodies or community expectations shape what is possible here?
Does the site have the resources, leadership engagement and readiness—commitment and efficacy—to implement now?
Who are the local opinion leaders, and what do they believe about the practice?
Who plans and leads locally, how will we reflect and adjust, and when do we evaluate?
understand.note: Hypothetical application; constructs summarized from Damschroder et al. (2009).

understand.text: Readiness, from Lesson 2, sits inside the inner setting. Weiner’s distinction travels well across borders: a site may lack commitment because the practice conflicts with local professional norms, or lack efficacy because training, language support or staffing is missing. The two call for different remedies.

challenge.text: Are national-culture frameworks valid at all? Brendan McSweeney argues that Hofstede’s claim to have identified national cultures rests on doubtful assumptions: that survey answers from employees of one multinational can represent a nation; that national culture is uniform within a country; and that it operates as a systematic cause of behavior. Hofstede replied in print, disputing the critique. The meta-analysis by Taras and colleagues offers a middle position: the dimensions do relate to outcomes, but modestly and unevenly, and less well than other predictors for behavior and performance. The defensible conclusion is calibrated use, not wholesale acceptance or dismissal.

items: **Frameworks are not forecasts.** CFIR is a determinant framework—a structured list of what might matter—not a model that predicts which sites will succeed. Its constructs are many, and teams can drown in them; choose the few most plausible for your setting.
**The evidence base is concentrated in health care.** CFIR was built from health-services research; its use in business and sport rests on analogy.

**Adaptation can become drift.** Local adaptation improves fit but can erode the components that produced results. Without an explicit list of core components, every site will “adapt” the hard parts away.
**Fidelity can become rigidity.** Insisting on identical forms across very different institutions can produce ceremonial adoption: the practice exists on paper and nowhere else.

challenge.title: Methodological note: the ecological fallacy and country scores

blocks.text: A country score on a cultural dimension is an average of survey responses. Inferring individual attitudes from group averages commits the *ecological fallacy*: a relationship that holds between countries need not hold between people within them, and may even reverse. Two countries can differ on average while most of their individuals overlap. For implementation, this means a country score cannot tell you how a particular site manager, coach or nurse will respond.

A second issue is the level of analysis. Meta-analytic correlations around .18 imply that cultural values explain a small share of variance in individual outcomes. That is not trivial across thousands of people, but it is far too weak to justify designing a site’s rollout around a national label. Measuring the site directly—its readiness, its institutions, its local leaders—is more informative and cheaper than you think.

apply.caption: Fidelity and adaptation: where to standardize and where to let sites decide (APERTURE teaching device, using CFIR’s core / periphery distinction)
cells: **Drift.** Each site reinvents the practice; results become uncomparable and often disappear.
**Hollow uniformity.** Same forms everywhere, but the active ingredient has been dropped.
**Adapted fidelity.** The active ingredients are protected; language, scheduling, roles and examples fit each site.
**Rigid fidelity.** Works where institutions resemble headquarters; invites ceremonial adoption elsewhere.

apply.text: A practical procedure: before rollout, write down the two to four components you believe produce the benefit and the evidence for each. Everything else—materials, meeting times, who facilitates, language, local examples—is periphery by default. Ask each site to propose its adaptations of the periphery and to report how it will measure the core. Review adaptations against the core list, not against headquarters’ habits.

apply.title: Executive twist: a single global scorecard

blocks.text: Headquarters wants one scorecard so sites can be ranked. Your sites differ in labor law, patient or customer mix, and staff tenure. A single ranking will reward the site whose institutions most resemble headquarters and invite gaming elsewhere. Refusing comparison entirely leaves the board blind. A defensible design reports the *core* indicators identically everywhere (so they are comparable), reports periphery measures locally, and adds context columns—turnover, regulatory constraints, start date—so that differences are read as information rather than as a league table.

apply.text: **Professional application.** Many professional baseball organizations run player development across a U.S. complex and an international academy, often in the Dominican Republic. Suppose a department rolls out a standardized development-plan process designed in the United States. Cultural averages will tempt explanations such as “players defer to coaches, so they won’t set their own goals.” A better diagnosis uses the frameworks in this lesson: institutional differences (education systems, family and trainer relationships, contract and visa timelines, the role of local staff), inner-setting readiness (are bilingual staff available to run the process, and do local coaches believe it helps?), and the core-versus-periphery question (is the core the written plan, or the weekly conversation in which the player and coach review progress against a measurable objective?). Local coaches who know the players and their families are frequently the people who can adapt the periphery without losing the core—and the people most likely to turn a ceremonial process into an internalized one.

retain.text: National-culture frameworks are weak priors: the meta-analytic evidence shows modest, uneven effects, and critics question whether a nation has a single culture at all. Institutions often explain more, and the real test of a transferred practice is whether it is internalized, not merely implemented. Frameworks such as CFIR structure the diagnosis; the core–periphery distinction tells you what to hold constant and what to let each site own.
Summarize the Taras et al. meta-analysis in two sentences, including one outcome that cultural values predict relatively well and one they predict poorly.
Draw the implementation–internalization matrix. Which quadrant would compliance audits fail to detect, and how would you detect it?
For a practice you might transfer between two sites, list its core components and three periphery elements you would let each site adapt.

takeaways: Cultural dimensions relate to work outcomes modestly and unevenly; use them as weak priors about groups, never as predictions about individuals.
Institutional distance—differences in rules, norms and shared assumptions—often explains rollout failure better than national culture.
Transfer succeeds when a practice is internalized, not just implemented; compliance metrics cannot detect ceremonial adoption.
CFIR structures diagnosis across five domains; decide the core components in advance and let sites adapt the periphery.

check.prompt: A site passes every audit of a new safety procedure—training completed, checklists filed—yet incident patterns are unchanged and staff describe the checklist as “paperwork for head office.” In Kostova’s terms, the practice is best described as:

glossary.definition: The difference between an organization’s stated strategic choices and the pattern of work, resource allocation and attention that actually follows.
A self-reinforcing loop in which pressure to meet targets diverts time from improvement, capability erodes, performance falls further, and leaders blame people rather than the system.
The recurring cadence of reviews—daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly—through which an organization notices deviations and makes decisions.
In Weiner’s definition, a shared psychological state combining change commitment and change efficacy among the members of an organization.
Members’ shared resolve to implement a change; strongest when they value it, weaker when they comply from obligation or lack of choice.
Members’ shared belief that they can carry out a change, based on their appraisal of task demands, resources and circumstances.
For a stable system over the long run, average work-in-process equals throughput multiplied by average time in the system (L = λW).
The number of items started but not yet finished in a system, such as open cases, contracts or patients.
The step in a process with the least capacity relative to demand; it sets the pace of the whole system.
The share of available time a resource is busy; with variability, waiting time rises steeply as utilization approaches 100 per cent.
A precise specification of how a task is done and what result it should produce, used as a hypothesis so that deviations become visible and can be investigated.
A measure of a behavior or condition believed to drive a later outcome, observable quickly enough to act on; its causal link should be tested.
A measure of the outcome an organization ultimately cares about, which arrives late and reflects many causes.
The degree of difference between two countries’ regulatory, cognitive and normative environments, which makes transferring organizational practices harder.
A practice carried out formally—forms filed, meetings held—while the people involved do not value it, so it produces little of its intended effect.
The distinction between the elements of an intervention believed to produce its benefit, which should be kept, and elements that can be tailored to each setting.
