The error of inferring individual characteristics or relationships from group-level averages, such as assuming a person holds their country’s average values.

exercise.title: Change Simulator

intro.text: You are the vice president of operations at Quillmore Health Partners, a fictional network of four community hospitals. The board has approved a new patient-flow system: a daily cross-department capacity huddle, a shared digital bed board as the single source of truth, and standard work for discharge planning beginning on day two of each stay. The chief executive wants it live before the winter surge. You will make six sequencing decisions over fourteen weeks.

Five indicators move with your choices: **adoption** (is the system actually used), **trust** (do staff believe leadership and the system), **operational stability** (are patients flowing safely while you change), **budget headroom** (implementation money left), and **momentum** (visible progress the executive team can see). Every path trades some of these against others. There is no single correct route; notice which indicators you protect instinctively and which you spend.
All people, hospitals and numbers are fictional. Effects are ordinal teaching heuristics (−2 to +2) grounded in this week’s readings, not predictions of what would happen in a real hospital.

text.text: “We have fourteen weeks until the surge. Eastbrook is keen, Linden Falls is solid, Saltmarsh’s physicians are skeptical, and Harrow is Harrow—high turnover and an admission system older than some of its nurses. I want all four live. How do you want to sequence it?”

choices.label: Big bang: train everyone and go live at all four hospitals in eight weeks.
choices.feedback: Simultaneous launch maximizes visible momentum and avoids a two-tier system, but it loads every site’s scarcest people at once, leaves no time to learn from a first site, and puts stability at risk at the weakest site.

choices.label: Pilot at Eastbrook for six weeks, then scale.
choices.feedback: A pilot protects stability and generates learning, but a pilot at the most enthusiastic, best-resourced site tests the system under the easiest conditions—results may not transfer.

choices.label: Run a four-week readiness diagnosis at every site, then decide the sequence.
choices.feedback: Diagnosing commitment and efficacy site by site shows people they were consulted and reveals which remedy each site needs, at the price of visible progress and the chief executive’s patience.

text.text: “Three sites are on track. Harrow isn’t. Half the night nurses haven’t been trained because we couldn’t release them from the floor, and the interface between the bed board and Harrow’s admission system drops updates for hours at a time.”

choices.label: Hold the date everywhere and deploy floating super-users to Harrow.
choices.feedback: You protect the timeline with money and borrowed experts, but the interface problem is technical, not a training gap; super-users cannot fix stale data.

choices.label: Go live at three sites; move Harrow back four weeks.
choices.feedback: Converting the big bang into a phased launch at the last moment protects the weakest site and signals that you listen, at a modest cost in momentum.

choices.label: Hold the date; Harrow runs a paper backup until the interface is fixed.
choices.feedback: A paper backup keeps the date but creates two sources of truth—the very problem the bed board was meant to solve—and tells Harrow staff the system is optional.

text.text: “Discharges before 11 a.m. are up from 14 to 31 per cent and average length of stay is down slightly. To be fair, we had a full-time coordinator funded by the pilot, and my managers volunteered for this.”

choices.label: Declare success and roll the Eastbrook playbook, unchanged, to the other three sites.
choices.feedback: Fast scaling captures momentum, but the pilot’s conditions—a funded coordinator and volunteer managers—will not exist elsewhere. Copying the form of a success without its conditions is a classic transfer error.

choices.label: Run a second pilot at Harrow before scaling.
choices.feedback: Testing at the hardest site reveals which components survive hostile conditions. It costs time and money, and the executive team may read it as hesitation.

choices.label: Scale now, but define the core (one board, discharge plan by day two) and let each site adapt the huddle format and timing.
choices.feedback: Separating core components from an adaptable periphery lets sites own the fit while protecting the active ingredients—if you can say clearly which parts are core.

text.text: Your diagnosis shows Eastbrook ready; Linden Falls ready, but changes to shift times require consultation with the nurses’ union; Saltmarsh nurses committed, physicians not (“another administrative initiative”); Harrow willing but short-staffed and without a reliable data interface. The chief executive reads it and says: “Useful. Now I need dates.”

choices.label: Sequence it: Eastbrook and Linden Falls first, Saltmarsh after physician engagement, Harrow after staffing and interface fixes.
choices.feedback: Matching sequence to readiness applies the right remedy to each site—efficacy support for Harrow, commitment work at Saltmarsh—while accepting that the last site will miss the surge.

choices.label: Launch everywhere on one date, with a site-specific support package for each.
choices.feedback: Tailored support uses the diagnosis without sacrificing the common date, but it is expensive and spreads your scarcest experts thinly across four launches.

choices.label: Give the chief executive the four-site launch she wants; you now know the risks.
choices.feedback: Knowing the risks does not remove them. Staff who were consulted and then overridden often trust leadership less than staff who were never asked.

text.text: “A patient was assigned to a bed the board showed as clean and empty. It was occupied. Nobody was harmed, but the story is everywhere, and night staff are saying the board is unsafe.”

choices.label: Pause the bed board at all sites until the data problem is fixed.
choices.feedback: Stopping to fix a safety-relevant defect is what the Toyota rules prescribe: a deviation is a failed hypothesis to investigate at once. The cost is visible momentum and an awkward board update.

choices.label: Keep going; publish a blameless incident review within 48 hours and fix the interface.
choices.feedback: Fast, transparent investigation treats the incident as information about the system rather than about individuals, which tends to build trust—provided the fix is real.

choices.label: Keep going; treat it as user error and schedule retraining.
choices.feedback: Attributing a system defect to the people using it is the attribution error at the heart of the capability trap. Staff who know the data were stale will conclude that leadership is not listening.

text.text: “We keep our own paper list. The board is two or three hours behind admissions, so if we trust it we send patients to beds that aren’t ready. Everyone does it. Nobody upstairs asked.”

choices.label: Ban parallel lists and start compliance audits of board use.
choices.feedback: Mandates raise measured adoption but push the workaround underground and remove the safety net staff built for a real defect. Compliance without belief is ceremonial adoption.

choices.label: Spend shifts on the floor with charge nurses, find the root cause (a three-hour sync), fix it, and allow paper lists until it is fixed.
choices.feedback: Going to where the work happens treats the workaround as evidence of a defect. Spear and Bowen describe exactly this: problems investigated where they occur, by the people doing the work, with a coach.

choices.label: Push a quick software patch and circulate Eastbrook’s early-win numbers.
choices.feedback: Early wins can sustain commitment, but advertising success while staff are living with a defect reads as spin. Short-term wins that avoid root causes are a known weakness of staged change models.

text.text: “Agency staffing costs have blown through forecast. I’m cutting thirty per cent of the remaining implementation budget. You decide where it comes from.”

choices.label: Cut the super-users and remaining training hours.
choices.feedback: Training and floor support are the efficacy side of readiness. Cutting them saves the most money and damages the sites least able to cope.

choices.label: Delay the final site by one quarter.
choices.feedback: Spreading the work out protects quality and limits work-in-process, at a visible cost to the timeline.

choices.label: Cut the planned analytics-dashboard features; keep the people.
choices.feedback: Protecting people over features signals what you think produces results. The executive team loses some reporting it wanted.

text.text: “The executive team wants one headline number: the percentage of discharges before 11 a.m. And I’d like it in unit managers’ bonus scorecards from next quarter.”

choices.label: Adopt it as the headline target, tied to bonuses.
choices.feedback: A single incentivized number focuses effort but invites gaming—discharging to a lounge, delaying admissions—and can hurt the lagging outcomes it was meant to proxy.

choices.label: Propose a balanced set reviewed weekly—leading (discharge plan by day two, board accuracy) and lagging (length of stay, readmissions, emergency-department boarding hours)—with no bonus link this year.
choices.feedback: Pairing leading and lagging indicators makes the causal assumption testable and lowers gaming pressure; the executive team gets less of a headline.

choices.label: Report the numbers only for learning; no targets this year.
choices.feedback: Learning-only measurement builds candor but can signal that the change is optional, and executives may withdraw attention.

text.text: “Your 8 a.m. huddle lands in the middle of shift handover. We run ours at 10:30 and use the board differently. Our numbers look worst in the network, but our beds turn over fine. I won’t make my nurses abandon handover to stand at a screen.” The chief executive asks you what you intend to do about Harrow.

choices.label: Enforce the standard: the huddle is at 8 a.m. everywhere.
choices.feedback: Uniform form is easy to audit, but if the timing conflicts with a real local constraint, staff will comply on paper and work around it in practice.

choices.label: Agree that time and format are periphery; Harrow keeps them if it meets the core measures (one board, plan by day two).
choices.feedback: Adapted fidelity: you hold the active ingredients constant and let the site own the rest, which requires that you measure the core and accept non-identical practice.

choices.label: Replace the manager with Eastbrook’s pilot coordinator.
choices.feedback: Replacing a dissenting local leader can unblock a site quickly, but it removes local knowledge and teaches every manager that objections are dangerous.

choices.label: Pause Harrow, fix staffing and the interface, and relaunch next quarter with Harrow’s staff designing the huddle.
choices.feedback: Addressing root causes before relaunch protects the weakest site and may produce a better design, at the cost of missing the surge there.

text.text: Six months later, every hospital holds an 8 a.m. huddle and audits show high board use. Harrow staff run a second, unofficial huddle at 10:30 where real decisions are made; the board is updated afterward to satisfy reports. Network averages look good. Whether patient flow has improved at Harrow is unclear, because the data no longer describe what happens. This is ceremonial adoption: implemented, not internalized.

Six months later, the four hospitals run recognizably different huddles but share one board and a discharge plan by day two. Comparison across sites is harder, and some executives complain about “four versions.” Board accuracy has risen at every site, and Harrow’s turnover of beds holds steady through the surge. The question you now face is whether you have defined the core correctly—or whether something important was left in the periphery.

Harrow’s metrics jump within a month under the new manager. Two experienced charge nurses resign; several others stop raising problems in the huddle. When the new manager returns to Eastbrook at the end of the year, Harrow’s numbers drift back. Elsewhere in the network, managers have learned that dissent carries a price, and the board receives fewer warnings about defects.

Harrow misses the winter surge on the new system and the chief executive is visibly frustrated. In the next quarter, with the interface fixed and two vacancies filled, Harrow’s staff design a 10:30 huddle that other sites later borrow. Adoption arrives late but appears durable. The board’s question is whether the lost quarter was worth it—an answer that depends on what the surge would have done to an unstable site.

debrief.text: Look back at your indicator profile. Most paths that maximize momentum early spend trust or stability, and most paths that protect trust spend momentum or budget. That is not a defect of the simulator; it is the central trade-off of implementation. The question is whether you spent each resource deliberately.

Three patterns recur across the paths. First, **sequencing is a bet about learning**: a pilot at an easy site buys momentum and teaches little about hard sites; a pilot at a hard site teaches more and looks slower. Second, **workarounds and near misses are data**: the choices that investigated where the work happens tended to build trust and stability, while mandates and “user error” explanations raised measured adoption and lowered trust. Third, **fidelity and adaptation are not opposites** when you specify the core and let sites own the periphery—but this only works if you can say, with evidence, which components produce the result.

These patterns reflect this week’s readings: readiness as commitment plus efficacy, the capability trap and its attribution error, Toyota’s treatment of deviations as experiments, and the core–periphery distinction in implementation science.

What the exercise does **not** show: real magnitudes, real probabilities, or the many ways a skilled leader could combine options that the menu does not offer. Indicator movements are ordinal heuristics written by APERTURE; a real rollout would require measuring them directly. Use your path as a mirror for your instincts—which indicator did you protect without thinking?—not as evidence about hospitals.

assumptions: All people, hospitals and figures are fictional; the pilot results are synthetic.
Effects are integers from −2 to +2 per choice, written as ordinal teaching heuristics grounded in the cited readings, not predictions.
Indicators start at zero and simply sum; the simulator does not model interactions between indicators or delays.
Each node offers a limited menu; real leaders can combine, modify or invent options.
Endings depend on your final decision; earlier decisions shape your indicator profile, not the ending text.

case.title: The International Initiative
case.fiction: All people, organizations and data in this case are fictional. Plant locations are used for realism only; nothing describes a real company, facility or labor agreement.

body.text: At 7:40 on a Tuesday morning, Marguerite Achterberg, chief operating officer of Tessaline Precision Components, read the customer’s audit letter for the third time. Tessaline makes machined and molded components for medical-device manufacturers. The letter, from its largest customer, cited a batch of housings from the company’s plant in Brno, in the Czech Republic, that had shipped with a dimensional defect the plant’s own checks should have caught. No patient had been harmed; the customer had caught the problem at incoming inspection. But the letter ended with a sentence Achterberg had underlined: the customer expected “a systemic corrective action across all Tessaline sites” within six months.

Tessaline runs three plants. Greenville, South Carolina, the oldest, employs about 520 people and houses headquarters. Santiago de los Caballeros, in a free-trade zone in the Dominican Republic, employs about 640 and has grown quickly over five years. Brno employs about 380, most of them skilled machinists and technicians, and came to Tessaline through an acquisition seven years ago. Each plant passes its quality audits. Each runs differently.

Achterberg already had an answer in mind. Eighteen months earlier, Greenville had piloted what the company called Tiered Daily Management: short daily huddles at three levels (cell, department, plant) that reviewed safety, quality, delivery and problems; standard work for setups and in-process checks; and a tablet-based escalation app that let any operator flag a problem, route it to the right engineer and track it to closure. The Greenville pilot had gone well (Exhibit 1). Achterberg wanted it in all three plants within six months, in identical form, so that the corrective-action response to the customer would be a single, auditable system.

She called the leadership group together that afternoon: Daniel Oduya, vice president of quality; Yolanda Peralta, general manager in Santiago; Tomáš Hrubý, general manager in Brno; Renée Castellanos, vice president of human resources; and Arjun Mehra, the chief financial officer. Achterberg opened with the letter and the deadline. “We have a system that works,” she said. “The customer wants it everywhere. I’d like to hear how we get it done, not whether.”

Oduya spoke first, and he supported a fast, uniform rollout. Regulators and customers in the medical-device business, he said, wanted documented, consistent processes; three versions of the system would mean three sets of procedures, three training records, three audit trails. “If an auditor asks why Brno’s escalation process differs from Greenville’s, ‘local culture’ is not an answer they will accept.” He did, however, add a caution: Greenville’s results had come with a new plant manager, two additional process engineers funded by the pilot, and a workforce that had chosen to volunteer for the first cells.

Peralta was supportive of the goals and worried about the form. Santiago’s annual operator turnover was around 35 per cent, much higher than at the other plants (Exhibit 2), because free-zone employers competed hard for the same workers. Most supervisors had been promoted from the line and were respected in part for knowing every job themselves. Operators, she said, rarely raised problems in open meetings with managers present; they told their supervisor privately, and the supervisor decided whether to escalate. “If we put a tablet in front of an operator and say ‘escalate directly to engineering,’ some will see it as going over the supervisor’s head. Some supervisors will see it that way too.” There was also a practical problem: for security reasons, personal phones were not allowed on the Santiago production floor, and the plant had a quarter of the tablets the app assumed. Training materials existed only in English.

Achterberg asked whether that was really about hierarchy or about the tablets. Peralta smiled. “Both. And about turnover. Half the people we train this spring will not be here next spring. Whatever we build has to work for someone in their second week.”

Hrubý was the most skeptical. Brno’s machinists were trained through a long technical apprenticeship tradition, he said, and they took pride in solving problems themselves at the machine. They had seen two previous corporate programs—a “Six Sigma belt” initiative and a reorganization into “value streams”—arrive with fanfare and disappear when the executives who championed them left. “My people will do the huddles if we tell them to. They will fill in the app. And they will think it is theater.” He also raised an institutional constraint: under the plant’s agreements and local practice, changes to shift start times and to how work was monitored required formal consultation with employee representatives, which typically took six to ten weeks. A daily huddle at the start of each shift would require moving shift start times by fifteen minutes.

Then Hrubý added something uncomfortable. The defective batch had not slipped through because operators failed to report problems. Two operators had noticed the dimension drifting and had adjusted the machine themselves, as they often did, without recording it. The in-process check had passed because it sampled after the adjustment. “We do not have a reporting problem,” he said. “We have a problem with a measurement plan that does not match how my people actually work.”

Castellanos, from human resources, worried about trust in Santiago. Two years earlier, a well-intentioned “speak-up” hotline launched from headquarters had led to the dismissal of a popular supervisor after an anonymous complaint, and operators still talked about it. She also noted that Brno’s and Santiago’s supervisors were evaluated on output and scrap; nothing in their objectives rewarded time spent on problem-solving. “If the huddle eats fifteen minutes of production every day and nobody changes the scorecard, supervisors will make the huddle shorter every week.”

Mehra, the chief financial officer, brought numbers. A full, identical rollout to both plants would cost roughly 1.9 million dollars over six months, mostly in tablets, software licenses, engineering time and training (Exhibit 3). The budget approved for corrective action was 1.4 million. He also pointed out that the customer had not asked for identical systems; it had asked for a systemic corrective action. “I would like someone to tell me which parts of this produced Greenville’s results, so we fund those first.”

Nobody could answer that precisely. Greenville had changed several things at once—the huddles, standard work, the app, the extra engineers, the new manager—and had measured outcomes, not the contribution of each component. Oduya thought standard work for in-process checks mattered most, given the Brno defect. Peralta suspected the daily cell huddle, run by supervisors, was the active ingredient. Hrubý thought the app was the least important element and the most likely to be resented.

Achterberg closed the meeting by asking each of them to send her a one-page view by Friday. Afterward she sat with the three exhibits and a blank page. She saw at least three defensible paths. She could roll out the full Greenville system identically and quickly, meeting the customer’s expectations of consistency and accepting the risk of ceremonial compliance. She could define a small set of core elements that every plant must implement and measure identically, and let each plant design the rest, which would require her to decide what the core was without clean evidence. Or she could sequence the rollout—Brno first, because of the defect, with its consultation process started immediately, and Santiago later, after redesigning the system for high turnover and a supervisor-centered escalation culture—and explain to the customer why a staged plan was more credible than a fast one.

Each path had a cost. A uniform rollout might satisfy auditors and fail operators. An adaptive one might look, to a customer reading quickly, like three plants doing their own thing. A sequenced one might miss the six-month expectation in at least one plant. And underneath all three lay Hrubý’s point: the defect that started everything might not be fixed by the system she was about to spend 1.4 million dollars deploying.

questions: Which components of Tiered Daily Management would you treat as core, and what evidence—from Exhibit 1 or elsewhere—supports each choice? What would you need to learn before you could be confident?

How much of the difference between the plants is national culture, and how much is institutions, history and local conditions (turnover, tablets, consultation, the hotline episode)? Why does the distinction matter for your design?
Hrubý argues the Brno defect was a measurement-plan problem, not a reporting problem. If he is right, what does that imply for the corrective action, and how would you test his claim quickly?

Design a sequence for the next six months within the 1.4 million budget. What are your decision points, and which leading indicators would tell you, at each plant, whether the system is being internalized rather than merely implemented?
How would you explain your chosen approach to the customer so that it reads as more credible, not less, than an identical rollout?

perspectives.title: Standardize fast for credibility
perspectives.text: In a regulated industry, consistency is part of the product. Roll out the full Greenville system identically, start Brno’s consultation immediately, fund Santiago’s translation and tablets first, and accept that some sites will initially comply more than they believe. Internalization can be built after the audit trail exists. The risk is ceremonial adoption and a costly system that does not address Brno’s actual failure mode.

perspectives.title: Hold the core, adapt the periphery
perspectives.text: Define two or three core elements—for example, standard work for in-process checks matched to how operators actually adjust machines, a daily cell-level problem review, and a single tracked record of every quality problem—and measure them identically everywhere. Let Santiago route escalation through supervisors and use paper or shared terminals; let Brno design the huddle with its employee representatives. Tell the customer what is common and why. The risk is choosing the wrong core without clean evidence.

perspectives.title: Fix the defect first, then sequence
perspectives.text: Treat the Brno failure as a hypothesis to test: redesign the in-process measurement plan with Brno’s machinists within weeks, which directly answers the customer. Then sequence the broader system—Brno after consultation, Santiago after a redesign for high turnover and a supervisor-centered escalation norm—and spend part of the budget on a proper comparison of components. The risk is that a staged plan looks slow to a customer expecting a single systemic action.

case.application: Player development organizations face the same structure when they move a development system between a U.S. complex and an international academy: a practice that worked under one set of conditions (staff, language, tenure, institutions) is expected to work identically elsewhere. The case’s questions transfer directly—which components are core, whether differences are cultural or institutional (turnover of young players, family and trainer relationships, bilingual staffing, contract timelines), and how to tell whether local coaches have internalized a process or are filling in forms for head office. The case also warns against assuming that a reporting or compliance tool fixes a problem whose real cause lies in how the work is actually done.

questions.prompt: A chief operating officer responds to slow execution by tightening the goal cascade so that every team’s objectives map precisely onto the corporate priorities. In light of Sull, Homkes and Sull’s argument, what is the most likely blind spot?

options.text: Teams will not understand the corporate priorities.
Vertical alignment is rarely the weak link; coordination across units that depend on each other is likely to remain the bottleneck.
The cascade will make the strategy too flexible.
Middle managers will have too much discretion.

questions.explanation: The authors argue that alignment up and down the hierarchy is usually adequate, while managers often cannot rely on colleagues in other functions and units. A tighter cascade strengthens what already works and leaves the cross-unit hand-offs untouched.

optionFeedback.a: Comprehension is a real issue in the article, but a cascade does not create it and is not the main blind spot here.
optionFeedback.c: A tighter cascade tends to reduce flexibility, not increase it.
optionFeedback.d: The article argues that middle managers need more, well-guided discretion, not less.

stimulus.text: A hypothetical customer-support organization misses its response-time target three months running. The director cancels the weekly knowledge-base improvement session (“we’re too busy”), approves overtime, and asks team leads for a list of the slowest individual agents. Response times improve for six weeks, then worsen past their original level as repeat contacts about the same unresolved issues rise.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis best fits this pattern?

options.text: The slowest agents are the problem; the director should replace them.
A capability trap: working harder produced a short-term gain while improvement work stopped, capability eroded, and attention shifted to blaming individuals.
Random variation: response times naturally fluctuate and nothing needs to change.
Insufficient urgency: the team needs a clearer burning platform.

questions.explanation: The sequence—cancelled improvement time, overtime, early gain, later decline driven by unresolved root causes, and a focus on individual agents—matches Repenning and Sterman’s capability trap. The remedy is to protect improvement time and examine the system, accepting a short-term cost.

optionFeedback.a: This is the attribution error in the trap: the rise in repeat contacts points to unresolved system problems, not individual effort.
optionFeedback.c: A gain followed by a decline past the starting level, with a clear mechanism (repeat contacts), is not well explained by noise.
optionFeedback.d: The team is already under intense pressure; more urgency would deepen the trap.

stimulus.text: Consultant’s slide: “Research shows 70% of change initiatives fail. Our clients’ initiatives succeed 85% of the time. Therefore, hiring us roughly triples your odds of success compared with going it alone.”

questions.prompt: What is the most fundamental flaw in this argument?

options.text: Eighty-five per cent is too high to be believable.
The 70 per cent base rate has no valid empirical source, and the 85 per cent figure uses an undefined, self-judged notion of success in a self-selected client group—so the comparison is meaningless.
The arithmetic is wrong: 85 per cent versus 30 per cent is not triple.
Consultants should never cite research.

questions.explanation: Hughes found no valid and reliable evidence for the 70 per cent figure. The consultant’s 85 per cent rests on its own definition of success, among clients who chose to hire it, so the two numbers share neither a definition nor a comparable population. The comparison cannot support a causal claim about the consultant’s effect.

optionFeedback.a: Implausibility is a hint, not the flaw; the problem is what the numbers measure and compare.
optionFeedback.c: Success odds of 85 vs 30 per cent are close to triple, so the arithmetic is roughly fine; the inputs are the problem.
optionFeedback.d: Citing research is fine; citing an unsupported statistic is the issue.

questions.prompt: A hospital unit wants a new electronic handover tool but doubts it can use it well. Which interventions primarily raise **change efficacy** (rather than commitment)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Protected practice sessions on real cases before go-live
A video of the chief executive explaining why the change matters
Super-users on each shift for the first two weeks
Temporarily reducing other documentation demands during launch
Sharing patient-safety stories that show the cost of the current process

questions.explanation: Efficacy depends on how people appraise task demands, resources and circumstances, so practice, on-shift support and reduced competing demands raise it. Leadership messaging and stories about the cost of the status quo work mainly on commitment, which this unit already has.

questions.prompt: A legal-operations team has 45 matters in progress and closes 9 per week. Leadership wants average lead time cut to 3 weeks without changing throughput. Using Little’s law, what is the maximum average number of matters that should be in progress?
questions.working: Current W = 45 ÷ 9 = 5 weeks. Target L = λ × W = 9 per week × 3 weeks = 27 matters in progress.
questions.explanation: Little’s law (L = λW) means that at constant throughput, lead time can fall only if work-in-process falls. Nine matters per week for three weeks implies 27 matters in progress, so the team must stop starting new matters until the backlog falls by 18.

stimulus.caption: Weekly capacity and demand in a hypothetical clinical laboratory

questions.prompt: Turnaround times are long and variable. You have budget for one action this quarter. What is the best next move?

options.text: Add a second intake shift to clear the morning backlog faster.
Protect analyzer time: pre-check samples at intake so none reach the analyzers defective, schedule maintenance outside peak hours, and stagger sample release.
Buy faster reporting software.
Raise all steps to 95 per cent utilization to match the analyzers.

questions.explanation: Analysis is the constraint, running at 95 per cent utilization, where waiting time rises steeply with any variability. Getting the most from the constraint—no defective inputs, no avoidable downtime, smoother arrivals—shortens queues without capital spending. Adding capacity elsewhere only moves more work into the bottleneck’s queue.

optionFeedback.a: More intake capacity feeds the analyzers faster and lengthens their queue; it does not raise output.
optionFeedback.c: Reporting has ample spare capacity; improving it changes almost nothing.
optionFeedback.d: High utilization everywhere would lengthen queues throughout; slack at non-bottlenecks absorbs variability.

stimulus.text: Fictional abstract: “Across 36 subsidiaries of one multinational, each in a different country, the national power-distance score correlated r = −.41 with the subsidiary’s annual number of employee improvement suggestions per 100 staff. We conclude that employees from high power-distance cultures are reluctant to make suggestions and recommend that suggestion systems be replaced with supervisor-led review in such countries.”

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest critique of the authors’ conclusion?

options.text: A correlation of −.41 is too small to matter.

The analysis is at the country level, so it cannot show how individual employees behave (ecological fallacy), and country scores are confounded with institutional differences—labor rules, management practices, subsidiary age—that could explain the pattern.
Thirty-six subsidiaries is too large a sample.
Power distance has been proven not to exist.

questions.explanation: A relationship between country averages does not license claims about individuals, and with one subsidiary per country, national culture is confounded with every institutional and organizational difference between sites. The recommendation might be right, but this design cannot show it; measuring readiness and obstacles at each site would.

optionFeedback.a: A correlation of that size across units can be meaningful; the problem is interpretation, not magnitude.
optionFeedback.c: Thirty-six units is small, not too large; the issue is design, not sample size.
optionFeedback.d: This overstates the critics; the meta-analytic evidence shows modest relationships, not none.

questions.prompt: You must decide which components of a multi-site practice are “core.” Rank these sources of evidence from most to least informative about whether a component causes the benefit.

options.text: A comparison of similar sites that adopted the component with sites that did not, measured before and after over the same period
A before-and-after comparison at one pilot site where several changes were made at once
The consensus of experienced managers who ran the pilot
Success stories published by the software vendor

questions.explanation: A comparison with similar non-adopting sites over the same period controls for trends and other concurrent changes, so it isolates the component best. A single-site before-and-after is confounded by everything else that changed. Manager consensus contains real knowledge but is vulnerable to motivated recall; vendor stories are selected for success and carry a commercial interest.

questions.prompt: A data team’s two analysts are busy 80 per cent of the time. Leadership proposes adding work until they are 95 per cent busy, “to get full value from them.” Using the single-server textbook queue as a guide, what should you expect?

options.text: Requests will wait about 20 per cent longer.
Waiting time will roughly stay the same, since the analysts were already busy.
Average waiting time will rise several-fold—in the textbook queue, from about 4 to about 19 times the average task length.
Waiting time will fall because the analysts will work more efficiently.

questions.explanation: In queues with variability, waiting time rises non-linearly as utilization approaches 100 per cent; in the single-server textbook queue, wait divided by task time equals u ÷ (1 − u), which goes from 4 at 80 per cent to 19 at 95 per cent. Real systems differ in magnitude but share the steep shape.

optionFeedback.a: This assumes waiting grows in proportion to utilization; it grows much faster near full load.
optionFeedback.b: The increase near full utilization is the steepest part of the curve.
optionFeedback.d: Busyness does not create efficiency; it removes the slack that absorbs variability.

stimulus.text: A hypothetical international NGO is scaling a maternal-health program from one country to two more. Evaluation at the first site suggested that monthly home visits by trained community health workers drove the benefit. Site A proposes replacing home visits with text-message reminders because travel is costly. Site B proposes running group sessions in the local language at a community center instead of the NGO’s office, and recruiting workers through local women’s associations.

questions.prompt: What is the best response, using the core–periphery distinction?

options.text: Approve both; local teams know their context best.
Reject both; fidelity requires identical implementation everywhere.
Treat home visits as core: work with Site A on reducing travel cost without dropping visits (or test the substitute rigorously), and approve Site B’s changes, which adapt the periphery.
Approve Site A to save money and reject Site B to keep the brand consistent.

questions.explanation: The evidence points to home visits as the active ingredient, so Site A’s proposal removes the core and should be resisted or tested before adoption. Site B changes language, venue and recruitment—periphery elements that improve fit without touching the core.

optionFeedback.a: Approving everything allows drift: Site A would drop the component believed to produce the benefit.
optionFeedback.b: Rigid fidelity blocks Site B’s sensible adaptations and invites ceremonial adoption.
optionFeedback.d: This reverses the logic: it sacrifices the core and protects the periphery.

questions.prompt: Your chief executive wants to open a company-wide change by saying “70 per cent of transformations fail, so resistance will not be tolerated.” In 150–200 words, write the private note you would send her proposing a different opening and explaining why. Use this week’s evidence on change failure rates, readiness and resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: I suggest we not open with the 70 per cent figure or with a warning about resistance. The statistic has no valid empirical source—an academic review traced it and found none—and some of our most respected people will check it; if they do, we lose credibility on day one. More important, our real risk is not defiance. Our survey and floor visits suggest two different problems: the warehouse teams want the new system but doubt they can learn it during peak season, while the account managers can use it but are not convinced it helps clients. The first is an efficacy problem that training time and support solve; the second is a commitment problem that evidence and involvement in design solve. Threatening resistance addresses neither and discourages the objections that will tell us where the design is wrong. I propose opening with what the current process costs us, in our own numbers, a clear statement of what will and will not change for people, and an invitation to flag problems early.

rubric.criterion: Evidence on the 70 per cent claim stated accurately and briefly
levels: 1 — notes that the claim lacks a valid empirical source and why that matters for credibility

rubric.criterion: Readiness diagnosis distinguishes commitment from efficacy with matched remedies
levels: 1 — distinguishes the two and matches a remedy to each

rubric.criterion: Treats resistance as information rather than only as defiance
levels: 1 — explains why objections should be invited and classified

rubric.criterion: Executive communication: clear recommendation, concise, respectful of the audience
levels: 0 — no clear alternative or overly long
1 — offers a specific alternative opening within the word range

reserve.prompt: Which piece of evidence most directly shows whether a newly announced strategic priority is real?

options.text: The number of times the chief executive mentions it in speeches
Whether people, money and recurring agenda time have been moved toward it from other uses
Employee survey agreement that the priority is important
Its placement on the first page of the strategy document

reserve.explanation: Realized strategy is the pattern of resource allocation. Reallocation of people, money and attention from other uses is costly and therefore credible; mentions, agreement and document placement are cheap signals.

optionFeedback.a: Mentions are communication, which Sull and colleagues show does not equal understanding or execution.
optionFeedback.c: Agreement shows awareness, not that anything has been resourced.
optionFeedback.d: Document placement costs nothing and changes nothing.

reserve.prompt: A hospital unit averages 30 inpatients and an average length of stay of 5 days. Using Little’s law, how many discharges per day does the unit average?
reserve.working: λ = L ÷ W = 30 patients ÷ 5 days = 6 discharges per day.
reserve.explanation: Little’s law, L = λW, can be rearranged to λ = L/W. With 30 patients in the unit on average and 5 days per stay, the unit must discharge about 6 patients per day in a stable state.

stimulus.text: Training slide: “Kurt Lewin’s scientifically validated three-step model—unfreeze, change, refreeze—proves that every successful change must follow these stages in order.”

reserve.prompt: What is wrong with this claim?

options.text: Lewin proposed five steps, not three.
Historical analysis suggests Lewin never developed the model in this form, and staged models are practitioner heuristics, not validated sequences that prove what every change must do.
The model applies only to manufacturing.
Nothing; the model is settled science.

reserve.explanation: Cummings, Bridgman and Brown argue that the three-step model took its familiar form after Lewin’s death, and no staged change model has been validated as a universal sequence. The slide overstates both pedigree and evidence.

optionFeedback.a: The issue is not the number of steps but the attribution and the claim of validation.
optionFeedback.c: Nothing restricts the model to manufacturing; the problem is its evidential status.
optionFeedback.d: This treats a practitioner heuristic as science.

stimulus.text: A hypothetical bank has rolled out a new client-onboarding process in five countries. The board wants a single league table ranking the countries by onboarding speed. Two countries have stricter identity-verification regulation; one has much higher staff turnover.

reserve.prompt: What is the best reporting design?

options.text: Publish the league table as requested; competition improves performance.
Refuse cross-country comparison because contexts differ.
Report core indicators identically for all countries alongside context (regulatory requirements, turnover, start date), and review differences as questions to investigate rather than as rankings.
Report only each country’s improvement against its own baseline, with no common indicators.

reserve.explanation: Comparable core indicators keep the board informed, while context columns stop institutional differences being read as performance differences. A raw league table would reward the countries with lighter regulation and invite gaming; refusing comparison leaves leadership blind.

optionFeedback.a: A raw ranking confounds performance with regulation and turnover and encourages gaming.
optionFeedback.b: Refusing all comparison removes useful information and looks evasive.
optionFeedback.d: Own-baseline reporting helps but abandons the comparable core the board legitimately needs.

assignment.title: A 90-Day Implementation Roadmap

brief.text: Choose a change you would plausibly want to introduce: a new organizational process, an analytical or information system, a meeting cadence, a development method, or a cross-department workflow. Keep it hypothetical and non-confidential—do not use real people, real teams or proprietary information. A fictional organization modelled on settings you know well is ideal.

Write a 90-day implementation roadmap that a skeptical senior executive could approve and a frontline manager could follow. The roadmap should show that you have diagnosed before prescribing, sequenced deliberately, and built in the feedback loops that tell you when to adjust. Use this week’s ideas explicitly: allocation evidence, readiness (commitment and efficacy), bottlenecks and work-in-process, leading and lagging indicators, and the core–periphery distinction.

Be honest about evidence. Where you rely on a practitioner heuristic, say so; where a causal assumption links a leading indicator to an outcome, state it as an assumption to be tested. All numbers should be labelled as estimates or synthetic.

assignment.deliverable: A written 90-day implementation roadmap (1,500–2,500 words) for a hypothetical change of your choosing, with a one-page phase table.

template.heading: Goal and case for change
template.guidance: What will be different in 90 days and in a year? What does the status quo cost, in local terms? Avoid borrowed statistics.

template.heading: Diagnosis
template.guidance: Allocation evidence (what must be reallocated), readiness by group (commitment and efficacy), the likely bottleneck, and institutional or site differences. Note what you do not know.

template.heading: Design: core and periphery
template.guidance: List the two to four core components and the evidence for each; list what sites or teams may adapt.

template.heading: Phases and sequencing
template.guidance: Days 1–30, 31–60, 61–90: activities, owners, dependencies, and why this order (pilot or not, where first, work-in-process limits).

template.heading: Stakeholders and communication
template.guidance: Who gains, who loses, who decides; what each group hears, when, from whom; how objections will be collected and classified.

template.heading: Operating rhythm and metrics
template.guidance: Meeting cadence; leading indicators (weekly) and lagging indicators (later), with the assumption linking them and how you will test it; gaming risks.

template.heading: Risks and decision points
template.guidance: A short risk register (likelihood, impact, mitigation) and two or three pre-committed decision points with the evidence that would trigger continue, adapt, pause or stop.

template.heading: Phase table
template.guidance: One-page table summarizing phases, milestones, owners, metrics and decision points.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Diagnosis uses allocation evidence, readiness by group, bottlenecks and institutional differences; uncertainties named and addressed.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Diagnosis covers most elements with reasonable evidence; some uncertainties named.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Diagnosis is generic or relies mainly on assumed resistance or culture.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Little or no diagnosis; the plan begins with the solution.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Core components justified with evidence; periphery explicit; phase order, dependencies and work-in-process limits clearly reasoned.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Core and phases defined with mostly sound reasoning; some dependencies implicit.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Phases listed but the reasoning for order or core is thin.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No meaningful sequencing; everything starts at once or order is arbitrary.

levels.label: Exemplary

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Main groups covered with tailored messages.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Generic communication plan; little differentiation.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: Stakeholders largely absent.

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Clear cadence; leading and lagging indicators paired with stated, testable causal assumptions; gaming risks addressed.

levels.label: Proficient

levels.label: Developing

levels.label: Beginning

rubric.criterion: Risks, decision points and evidence honesty

levels.label: Exemplary
levels.descriptor: Specific risks and mitigations; pre-committed decision points with triggers; heuristics and estimates labelled honestly.

levels.label: Proficient
levels.descriptor: Risks and decision points present; most claims appropriately labelled.

levels.label: Developing
levels.descriptor: Risks generic; decision points vague; some heuristics presented as fact.

levels.label: Beginning
levels.descriptor: No risk thinking; claims overstated.

prompts: Think of a change you led or lived through that stalled. Using Lesson 1’s audit, what was never reallocated, and which hand-off between units failed?
In the Change Simulator, which indicator did you protect without thinking—momentum, trust, stability or budget? What does that suggest about your default instincts as a leader?
Where have you explained a person’s or a site’s behavior by national or regional culture when institutions, incentives or resources might explain it better? What would you look at now?
In environments you know across the U.S. and Latin America, which elements of a development or operating process would you treat as core, and which would you let local staff adapt?

review.front: What is the best evidence that a strategic priority is real?
review.back: Reallocation of people, money and recurring agenda time toward it from other uses—not speeches, documents or survey agreement.

review.front: According to Sull, Homkes and Sull, which is usually weaker: vertical alignment or cross-unit coordination?
review.back: Cross-unit coordination. Alignment up and down the hierarchy is usually adequate; few managers can always rely on colleagues in other units.

review.front: Describe the capability trap in one sentence.
review.back: Pressure to hit targets crowds out improvement time, capability erodes, performance falls further, and leaders blame people, increasing pressure.

review.front: What did Hughes (2011) conclude about the claim that 70 per cent of change initiatives fail?
review.back: There is no valid and reliable empirical evidence for it; the cited sources do not support a general failure rate.

review.front: What is the evidential status of Kotter’s eight steps?
review.back: A practitioner heuristic drawn from the author’s observations—useful as a checklist, not a tested sequence.

review.front: What do Cummings, Bridgman and Brown argue about Lewin’s three-step model?
review.back: Lewin never developed the unfreeze–change–refreeze model in its familiar form; it took shape after his death.

review.front: Weiner’s two components of readiness for change?
review.back: Change commitment (shared resolve) and change efficacy (shared belief in collective capability). Each needs different remedies.

review.front: Three types of objection to classify before responding?
review.back: Content (the design may be wrong), process (people were not consulted or informed), consequences (status, workload, security). Only content objections should change the design.

review.front: State Little’s law and one managerial implication.
review.back: L = λW. At constant throughput, lead time falls only if work-in-process falls—stop starting, start finishing.

review.front: Why does adding capacity at a non-bottleneck rarely help?
review.back: Output is limited by the constraint; extra capacity elsewhere adds idle time or queue in front of the bottleneck.

review.front: In Spear and Bowen’s account, why does rigid specification of work enable flexibility?
review.back: Specified work is a hypothesis; deviations are immediately visible and investigated as experiments, so the system learns and adapts.
Leading: an actionable, early measure of behavior believed to drive the outcome. Lagging: the outcome itself, late and multi-caused. The link must be tested.

review.front: What did the Taras, Kirkman and Steel meta-analysis find about Hofstede’s dimensions?
review.back: Modest relationships with work outcomes (about .18 overall), stronger for emotions and attitudes than behavior and performance, and stronger in tighter cultures.

review.front: Kostova: what does transfer success require?
review.back: Institutionalization—the practice is both implemented and internalized (valued) at the receiving unit. Implementation alone can be ceremonial.
Holding the core components constant and measured everywhere while letting each site adapt the periphery (timing, language, format, roles).

preview.text: Implementation decisions are rarely only operational: the choice to standardize, to pause a site, to tie bonuses to a metric, or to replace a dissenting manager carries ethical and governance consequences. Week 13 turns to those responsibilities—decision rights, unintended consequences and institutional trust. In Week 14, this week’s roadmap becomes the capstone’s change-management strategy and first 90-day plan.
